Legalese is the special style of language used in legal documents — things like contracts, laws, court rulings, terms and conditions, and official legal notices. It is not a separate language, but it is a very specific way of writing English (or any language) that is deliberately formal, highly technical, and often very difficult for ordinary people to understand.

Think of it this way: a doctor might say "myocardial infarction" when a regular person would just say "heart attack." Legalese works the same way — it uses complex, specialised words and sentence structures where plain, simple language could often do the same job.
What legalese actually looks and feels like

When you read a legal document and feel confused, overwhelmed, or like you need a specialist to translate it for you — that's legalese at work. Here are the main things that make writing "legalese":

Very long, tangled sentences. A single sentence in a legal document can go on for an entire paragraph, with clause after clause piled on top of each other. Lawyers do this to try to cover every possible situation in one statement, leaving no gap for misinterpretation.

Archaic (old-fashioned) words and phrases. Legalese is full of words that most people stopped using in everyday speech centuries ago. Words like hereinafter (meaning "from this point forward in this document"), whereas (used to introduce background facts), heretofore (meaning "before now"), therein, thereof, hereto, aforesaid, and witnesseth are classic examples. These feel ancient because many of them genuinely are — they were frozen into legal writing long ago and simply never left.

Latin phrases. Legal writing borrows heavily from Latin, since Western law has deep roots in Roman legal tradition. Phrases like habeas corpus, prima facie, mens rea, bona fide, per se, and inter alia appear regularly. A non-lawyer reads these and is immediately at a disadvantage.

Paired synonyms (doublets and triplets). Legalese has a strong habit of saying the same thing twice or three times in a row using near-synonyms, just to make sure nothing slips through a loophole. You'll see phrases like "null and void," "cease and desist," "terms and conditions," "aid and abet," and "acknowledge and agree." This practice dates back to a time when English courts used both English and French words to make documents enforceable across both languages — but the habit stuck long after the need disappeared.

Extremely precise, technical definitions. In legalese, ordinary words are often given very specific legal meanings that differ from everyday usage. The word "consideration" in casual speech means simply thinking about something. In contract law, it means something of value exchanged between parties. The word "party" doesn't mean a celebration — it means a person or entity involved in a legal agreement. This precision is intentional, because in law, words carry enormous consequences.

Passive voice and impersonal tone. Legal writing tends to avoid saying who is doing what directly. Instead of "You must pay within 30 days," legalese might say "Payment shall be rendered within a period not to exceed thirty (30) days from the date hereof." This impersonal, detached tone is a hallmark of the style.

Numbers written twice. You'll often see something like "thirty (30) days" or "five hundred dollars ($500)" — the number written in both words and numerals. This is a precaution against misreading, since changing a word is harder to miss than changing a digit.

Legalese did not appear out of nowhere. It developed for genuine reasons, even if many of those reasons are no longer as relevant today.

The biggest reason is precision and certainty. Law is an arena where the exact meaning of a single word can determine who wins a court case, who owes money, who goes to prison, and who gets property. Lawyers historically developed very specific, tested language to minimise ambiguity. If a phrase has been used in courts for two hundred years and its meaning is well-established, lawyers are reluctant to swap it for a simpler phrase whose legal interpretation is untested.

Another reason is comprehensiveness. Legal documents try to anticipate every possible situation, exception, and edge case. This is why they are so long and complex — they are trying to leave nothing undefined.

There is also an element of professional tradition. Lawyers are trained in law schools where they read legal documents written in legalese, and they produce legal documents written in legalese. The style is self-perpetuating across generations of legal professionals.

Finally — and this is a more uncomfortable truth — legalese can also serve as a barrier to entry. When only trained professionals can understand legal documents, ordinary people become dependent on those professionals. This gives lawyers a kind of power and economic value that plain language might reduce.

The most significant criticism of legalese is that it excludes the very people it is supposed to serve. Laws exist to govern citizens, contracts exist between ordinary people, and terms of service exist for everyday users — yet the language used in all of these is frequently incomprehensible to the average person without legal training.

Consider something as common as the terms and conditions you click "I agree" to when you sign up for an app or website. Technically, you are bound by everything in that document. But most people have no realistic ability to understand what they've agreed to, because it's written in dense legalese. This creates an imbalance of power: one side (the company with its legal team) understands the document fully; the other side (the individual user) does not.

This problem can have very serious real-world consequences. People sign contracts without understanding clauses that limit their rights. Tenants miss critical terms in leases. Patients sign medical consent forms packed with legal language. In all these cases, legalese works against the people it's supposed to inform.
The push against legalese: Plain Language

There is a growing and well-established movement called the Plain Language Movement, which argues that legal documents should be written in clear, simple, accessible language that an ordinary person can read and understand. Many governments around the world have even passed laws requiring government communications and public-facing legal documents to be written in plain language.

The core argument is this: precision and clarity are not enemies. A document can be legally accurate and clearly written. You don't need to say "the party of the first part hereinafter referred to as the Lessor" when you can simply say "the landlord." You don't need "cease and desist" when "stop" works just as well. You don't need "in the event that" when "if" does the same job in two fewer words.

Lawyers who support plain language argue that simpler writing actually reduces disputes, because both parties genuinely understand what they agreed to — which is, after all, the whole point of a contract.

The word itself is used with a slightly negative, sometimes mocking tone. When someone says "it was written in legalese," they almost always mean it as a complaint — a signal that the document was needlessly complex, difficult to read, or deliberately obscure. It carries the implication that the language is an obstacle rather than a tool.

You might hear it used like this: "I tried to read the rental agreement, but it was pure legalese — I couldn't make sense of it." Or: "Can you translate this contract from legalese into plain English for me?"

The "-ese" suffix (like in "journalese," "corporatese," or "bureaucratese") is typically used to describe language varieties that are seen as overly jargon-heavy, impenetrable, and used by a particular professional group — often with a sense that the complexity is excessive or unnecessary.

Legalese is the dense, formal, technical style of writing found in legal documents. It is characterised by archaic vocabulary, Latin phrases, long sentences, paired synonyms, and highly technical definitions of ordinary words. It developed out of a genuine need for legal precision and comprehensiveness, but it has been widely criticised for making legal documents inaccessible to ordinary people. The word "legalese" itself is almost always used critically, to describe writing that is unnecessarily complex and difficult for a non-specialist to understand.
